density at the initial time, which may be a delta function (deterministic initial condition) or any valid pdf. transformation: the fokker-planck equation ∂p(x,t)/∂t = −∂/∂x[μ(x,t)·p(x,t)] + (1/2)·∂²/∂x²[d(x,t)·p(x,t)] where d(x,t) = σ²(x,t) is the diffusion coefficient drift term −∂/∂x[μ·p] deterministic advection diffusion term +(1/2)·∂²/∂x²[d·p] random spreading probability conservation ∫p(x,t)dx = 1 total probability preserved output space probability density function p(x, t) ≥ 0 ∀x,t with ∫₋∞^∞ p(x,t) dx = 1 a time-parameterized family of probability density functions over state space. each p(x,t) encodes the complete statistical state of the system at time t. assumptions / preconditions required • markov property: future depends only on present state • continuous sample paths (no jumps) • ito interpretation of stochastic integrals • sufficient smoothness of μ(x,t), σ(x,t) implicit • gaussian increments (from wiener process) • infinitesimal variance grows linearly with dt • no long-range temporal correlations section 03 interactive simulation observe how the probability density evolves under different drift and diffusion parameters. compare individual particle trajectories with the ensemble behavior. probability density p(x,t) particle trajectories parameters drift (μ) 0.0 deterministic velocity component diffusion (d) 0.5 random spreading rate particles 50 number of sample trajectories reset pause mean e[x(t)] 0.00 variance var[x(t)] 0.25 entropy h[p] 0.00 time 0.00 intuition mathematical edge cases building intuition think of smoke dispersing in air. the drift term is like wind pushing the smoke in a preferred direction. the diffusion term is the natural spreading of smoke particles due to random molecular motion. the fokker-planck equation tells you exactly how the "density cloud" evolves over time — not where individual particles go, but how the overall distribution changes shape. mathematical structure ∂p/∂t = −∂j/∂x (continuity equation) j = μ·p − (1/2)·∂(d·p)/∂x (probability current) the equation has the structure of a conservation law. probability is neither created nor destroyed, only transported. the probability current j describes the flow of probability mass through state space. stationary solution ∂p/∂t = 0 ⟹ j = const gaussian case μ, d const → p ∝ exp(−(x−μt)²/2dt) edge cases & limits pure diffusion (μ = 0) distribution spreads symmetrically. variance grows linearly: var(t) = 2dt. the distribution approaches gaussian by central limit theorem. pure drift (d = 0) deterministic translation. all probability mass moves with velocity μ. the distribution shape is preserved exactly. absorbing boundaries when p = 0 at boundaries, probability "leaks" out. total probability decreases. models first-passage-time problems. section 04 mechanism operational structure 1 parse stochastic dynamics extract drift μ(x,t) and diffusion d(x,t) coefficients from the sde formulation 2 construct probability current j = μ·p − (1/2)·∂(d·p)/∂x combines deterministic flow and diffusive spreading 3 apply conservation law ∂p/∂t = −∂j/∂x ensures probability is conserved (for natural boundaries) 4 solve pde with initial/boundary conditions analytical solutions exist for special cases; numerical methods for general case constituent components primitive: wiener process the mathematical abstraction of brownian motion. independent gaussian increments: dw ~ n(0, dt) e[dw] = 0, var[dw] = dt primitive: ito calculus the integration theory for stochastic processes. contains the ito correction term (−½σ²∂²f/∂x²dt) df = (∂f/∂x)μ dt + (∂f/∂x)σ dw primitive: continuity equation conservation law from fluid dynamics. applied here to probability mass instead of fluid mass. ∂ρ/∂t + ∇·j = 0 epistemic dependency graph section 04.5 information profile what is preserved total probability ∫p(x,t)dx = 1 always maintained (with natural boundaries) markov structure the evolution is memoryless — p(x,t) contains all information needed for future prediction moment hierarchy if initial condition has finite moments, they remain computable from p(x,t) stationary distribution (if exists) for ergodic systems, converges to unique equilibrium distribution what is destroyed individual trajectories no information about which specific path a particle took — only ensemble statistics remain temporal correlations the pdf at time t contains no information about correlations across time initial conditions (eventually) for ergodic systems, all memory of initial distribution is lost at stationarity higher-order structure multi-time correlations and path-dependent quantities require the full path measure section 05 validation & limits correctness criteria theoretical • consistency with underlying sde (kolmogorov equivalence) • non-negativity preservation: p(x,t) ≥ 0 • normalization: ∫p(x,t)dx = 1 for all t • convergence to stationary distribution (if ergodic) empirical validation observable checks • monte carlo simulation of sde — compare histograms • moment matching: e[xⁿ](t) from pde vs simulation • first-passage-time statistics • stationary distribution measurements failure modes jump processes discontinuous jumps require the kolmogorov-feller equation instead. the fokker-planck equation assumes continuous paths. non-markovian memory fractional brownian motion, colored noise, and other processes with memory require extended formalisms. singular coefficients when d(x) → 0 or μ(x) has singularities, solutions may not exist or be non-unique. scope of applicability valid domains • diffusion in potential landscapes • thermal fluctuations in physical systems • financial models (black-scholes framework) • neural stochastic dynamics • population genetics (genetic drift) • chemical kinetics (stochastic reactions) outside scope • lévy flights (infinite variance jumps) • turbulent transport (non-gaussian statistics) • quantum measurement processes • discrete state markov chains • deterministic chaos • multi-fractal processes section 06 diagnostic questions what happens if the markov assumption is violated? − the fokker-planck equation fundamentally relies on the markov property — that the future depends only on the present state, not on the path taken to reach it. when memory effects exist (e.g., viscoelastic media, fractional dynamics), the fokker-planck equation produces incorrect predictions. the actual distribution will differ systematically from the pde solution. alternative: generalized fokker-planck equations with memory kernels, or path integral formulations. which invariant does this tool rely on most critically? + the conservation of probability is the foundational invariant. this is expressed mathematically as the continuity equation structure: ∂p/∂t + ∂j/∂x = 0 this ensures probability is neither created nor destroyed — it merely flows through state space. any numerical scheme that violates this produces unphysical results. can two different sdes produce identical fokker-planck equations? + no — the mapping from ito sde to fokker-planck equation is unique. given an sde: dx = μ(x,t)dt + σ(x,t)dw the drift μ and diffusion d = σ² are uniquely determined. however, different stochastic calculi (stratonovich vs ito) can lead to different fokker-planck forms for the same physical system. physical interpretation matters: the choice of calculus must match the physical noise interpretation. what is the relationship to the backward kolmogorov equation? + the fokker-planck (forward) equation evolves the probability density forward in time. the backward equation evolves expectations backward in time: forward (fokker-planck) ∂p/∂t = l†p backward (kolmogorov) −∂u/∂s = lu where l is the generator and l† its adjoint. the forward equation answers "where will the system be?"; the backward answers "from where did it come?" or computes expected hitting times. when does the fokker-planck equation have a closed-form solution? + closed-form solutions exist for limited cases: 1. constant μ and d → gaussian solution 2. linear drift μ(x) = −αx, constant d → ornstein-uhlenbeck process 3. certain potential landscapes → separation of variables for general cases, numerical methods (finite difference, finite element, spectral methods) are required. section 07 comparative position tool input output use case fokker-planck sde coefficients time-dependent pdf distribution evolution master equation transition rates discrete state probabilities jump processes langevin dynamics force field sample trajectories simulation path integral action functional path probability weight rare events kramers-moyal jump moments pde expansion non-diffusive processes when to prefer • need full distributional information over time • analytical treatment is possible • studying stationary distributions • computing first-passage statistics • system is low-dimensional (1d-3d) when to avoid • high-dimensional systems (curse of dimensionality) • need individual trajectory statistics • non-markovian or non-gaussian processes • discrete state spaces • jump processes with large jumps headings.text: What epistemic element type does this instance belong to?
Treating λ as a property of the world

notes.text: poisson distribution — epistemic tool episte cnica catalog ◐ light notes / live / pd poisson distribution live note interactive #poisson #simulation a discrete probability distribution that transforms observations of rare event counts into probabilistic claims about reality's rate structure. index formulation — element type, instance, function identity — name, type, summary formal characterization — pmf, properties assumptions & preconditions — independence, rate mechanism & simulation — interactive sampling epistemic role — function, preservation, loss validation & failure modes — correctness, empirical scope & limits — domains, comparison diagnostic questions — assumptions, invariants cognitive friction — misunderstandings references — schema formulation what epistemic element type does this instance belong to? concrete epistemic artifact — a probabilistic claim about one count dataset's rate structure — produced by applying an epistemic operator (the poisson pmf with rate λ), and usable as an epistemic standard (limit-theorem, maximum-entropy, and consistency checks). schema: philosophia artium epistemicarum et operis . what is this epistemic instance? p(x = k) = e −λ · λ k / k!, mapping a rate parameter λ to a distribution over non-negative integer counts, assuming events occur independently at constant average rate. type: generative / inferential probability model — named after siméon denis poisson (1837). what grounds this reading? it resolves the epistemic gap between observing discrete counts and needing probabilistic predictions — summarizing rate information while quantifying uncertainty. it preserves the expected count, additivity, and independence structure; it destroys temporal structure, event characteristics, and causal dependencies. 01 identity name poisson distribution named after siméon denis poisson (1837) type generative / inferential belongs to the class of probability models — tools that encode uncertainty about observables through parametric structures. one-line summary maps a rate parameter λ to a probability distribution over non-negative integer counts, assuming events occur independently at constant average rate. epistemic insight the poisson distribution is not merely a formula — it is a compression device that reduces infinite possible temporal event patterns into a single scalar λ, preserving only the rate information while discarding all temporal structure. 02 formal characterization probability mass function p(x = k) = e -λ · λ k / k! λ rate parameter (expected count) k observed count (k ∈ {0, 1, 2, ...}) e euler's number (~2.718) input space single positive real number λ ∈ ℝ⁺ representing the expected number of events per unit interval (time, space, etc.) output space probability distribution over non-negative integers ℤ⁺₀ with infinite but countable support. transformation t: ℝ⁺ → δ(ℤ⁺₀) maps rate to probability distribution over counts. interactive pmf λ = k (count) mean: 4 | variance: 4 | mode: 3, 4 key properties mean (e[x]) λ variance (var(x)) λ equidispersion e[x] = var(x) skewness 1/√λ mode ⌊λ⌋ and ⌈λ⌉ - 1 additive property if x₁ ~ poisson(λ₁) and x₂ ~ poisson(λ₂) are independent: x₁ + x₂ ~ poisson(λ₁ + λ₂) this property enables aggregation of counts across intervals while preserving distributional form. 03 assumptions & preconditions stationarity the rate λ remains constant throughout the observation period. event probability does not change over time or space. required independence the occurrence of one event does not affect the probability of another. no clustering or contagion effects. required rarity (at infinitesimal scale) in very small subintervals, the probability of more than one event is negligible. events occur one at a time. required epistemic warning these assumptions are rarely perfectly satisfied in real-world data. the poisson distribution is best understood as an idealization — a useful approximation whose validity must be assessed, not assumed. 04 mechanism & simulation observe how poisson-distributed events emerge from a constant-rate process. each simulation generates events over time intervals, demonstrating the relationship between λ and observed counts. rate (λ events/unit time) 1 5 15 intervals 5 20 50 run simulation event timeline each dot represents an event occurrence over time count distribution count (k) sample mean: — law of large numbers observe sample mean converging to λ as observations accumulate reset sample size (n) |sample mean - λ|: — 05 epistemic role function the poisson distribution resolves the epistemic gap between: → observing discrete counts and needing probabilistic predictions → summarizing rate information while quantifying uncertainty → enabling inference from partial observations to population parameters preservation profile expected count — λ is preserved as both mean and variance additivity — counts can be summed while preserving distribution independence structure — assumed and propagated forward destruction / loss profile × temporal structure — when events occurred is lost × event characteristics — magnitude, duration, severity × causal dependencies — why events occurred × rate variation — fluctuations in λ over time × overdispersion — variance exceeding mean × zero-inflation — excess zeros beyond model 06 validation & failure modes correctness empirical failures formal correctness criteria limit theorem poisson arises as limit of binomial(n, p) as n → ∞, p → 0, np → λ. this provides mathematical grounding for the "rare events" interpretation. maximum entropy among all distributions with fixed mean on non-negative integers, poisson has maximum entropy. it makes minimal additional assumptions. consistency the sample mean converges to λ almost surely (slln), providing consistent estimation. empirical validation methods dispersion test check if variance ≈ mean (equidispersion holds) sample mean sample variance test chi-square goodness of fit compare observed frequencies with expected frequencies under poisson model. systematic failure modes overdispersion when variance > mean. common in clustered data, mixed populations, or when independence fails. alternative: negative binomial underdispersion when variance alternative: generalized poisson, com-poisson zero-inflation excess zeros beyond what poisson predicts. common in "hurdle" scenarios or structural zeros. alternative: zero-inflated poisson (zip) 07 scope & limits valid domains • radioactive decay events • phone calls at a call center • website hits per minute • typographical errors per page • mutations in dna sequences • arrivals at a queue questionable domains • disease outbreaks (contagion) • traffic accidents (clustering) • insurance claims (catastrophes) • crime statistics (hot spots) • ecological counts (aggregation) structural limits • cannot model bimodality • single parameter limits flexibility • requires constant rate • no memory of past events • integer-only support comparative position tool parameters variance/mean when to use poisson λ = 1 rare, independent events binomial n, p < 1 fixed number of trials negative binomial r, p > 1 overdispersed counts geometric p > 1 waiting time until success 08 diagnostic questions what happens if the rate λ varies over time? if the rate varies, you're no longer dealing with a single poisson process. the aggregate will typically show overdispersion — variance exceeds mean. this is because: var(total) = e[var(x|λ)] + var(e[x|λ]) = e[λ] + var(λ) > e[λ] the mixture of poissons with varying λ creates a compound distribution with greater spread. can two different processes produce indistinguishable count distributions? yes. this is an identifiability problem. given only count data, you cannot distinguish between: a homogeneous poisson process with rate λ a mixture of poisson processes with varying rates averaging to λ a process with clustered arrivals that happen to match the count distribution the count distribution alone is insufficient to recover the underlying process structure. what invariant does poisson rely on most critically? the equidispersion invariant : e[x] = var(x). this is the signature property that distinguishes poisson from other count distributions. when this invariant fails: overdispersion → model underestimates variability underdispersion → model overestimates variability checking this invariant is the first diagnostic for poisson appropriateness. how does sample size affect poisson inference? with larger samples: estimate precision improves (∝ 1/√n) but assumption violations become more detectable small departures from poisson become statistically significant paradoxically, large samples can make poisson less applicable — not because the model is more wrong, but because you can detect smaller departures from it. 09 cognitive friction systematic misunderstandings confusion between artifact and reality the poisson distribution describes our representation of uncertainty, not the underlying generative process. real events don't "follow" a poisson — our model assumes independence and constant rate as useful approximations. misinterpretation of assumptions as facts independence and stationarity are assumed , not discovered. they are simplifying choices that make the model tractable, not empirical truths to be accepted uncritically. overextension beyond scope applying poisson to bounded counts (can't exceed n), heavy-tailed phenomena (power law distributions), or clustered data violates core assumptions. the model's simplicity invites overuse. treating λ as a property of the world λ is an epistemic parameter — a summary of our expectations — not an ontological feature. different observers with different information may legitimately use different λ values for the same phenomenon. references philosophia artium epistemicarum et operis — schema of this page: does this instance belong to? concrete epistemic artifact — a computed dispersion claim about one dataset — produced by applying an epistemic operator (the σ formula over squared deviations), and usable as an epistemic standard (normal-interval and failure-mode checks). schema: philosophia artium epistemicarum et operis . what is this epistemic instance? σ = √(σ(xᵢ − μ)² / n): the root-mean-square deviation from the arithmetic mean — the "typical distance" of points from center, built from three constituents (mean, squared deviation, square root). type: compressive / diagnostic descriptive statistic within the epistemic toolbox. what grounds this reading? it resolves the epistemic gap of mean reliability — without dispersion measures, central tendency is epistemically incomplete. it preserves relative ordering of distances, magnitude relationships, and the same units as the original data; it destroys direction of deviations, distribution shape, individual observation positions, and temporal ordering. 01 identity type classification compressive / diagnostic standard deviation belongs to the class of descriptive statistics — it compresses a distribution of values into a single scalar that characterizes spread, enabling diagnostic assessment of data homogeneity. one-line summary σ = √(σ(xᵢ - μ)² / n) transforms a collection of observations into a single scalar representing the root-mean-square deviation from the arithmetic mean — quantifying the "typical distance" of points from center. epistemic role resolves uncertainty about the reliability of the mean as a representative value. without dispersion measures, central tendency is epistemically incomplete. preserves relative ordering of distances, magnitude relationships, and (crucially) the same units as the original data — enabling direct interpretation. destroys direction of deviations (always positive), distribution shape (skew, modality), individual observation positions, and temporal ordering. 02 formal characterization transformation mapping 𝒯 : ℝⁿ → ℝ₊ | (x₁, x₂, ..., xₙ) ↦ σ input space (𝒜ᵢₙ) → a finite set of n real-valued observations → measurements on an interval or ratio scale → no requirement on distribution shape output space (𝒜ₒᵤₜ) ← a single non-negative real number ← in the same units as input observations ← bounded: σ = 0 iff all values identical computational decomposition interact with each step to observe the transformation pipeline. click on data points to modify the input. step 1 xᵢ raw data step 2 μ = σxᵢ/n mean step 3 (xᵢ - μ) deviations step 4 (xᵢ - μ)² squared diffs step 5 σ = √(σ/n) result reset randomize n = 8 μ = 0.00 σ = 0.00 03 mechanism constituent 1 arithmetic mean the centroid of the data — the point that minimizes the sum of squared deviations. sd is meaningless without this reference point. constituent 2 squared deviation squaring achieves two goals: it removes sign (direction) and disproportionately penalizes larger deviations — making sd sensitive to outliers. constituent 3 square root returns the measure to original units, enabling direct interpretation. without it, we would have variance (σ²) which is harder to interpret. outlier sensitivity analysis drag the outlier point to observe how standard deviation responds compared to other measures. note the quadratic sensitivity to extreme values. outlier position sd 1.00 mad 0.74 iqr 1.35 04 interactive playground distribution builder click on the canvas to add points. observe how sd changes with distribution shape. clear all σ = — distribution comparison adjust spread to compare identical means with different dispersions. low σ 1.0 high σ 3.0 normal distribution & the 68-95-99.7 rule for normally distributed data, standard deviation defines probability intervals. adjust σ to see how coverage changes. ±1σ ±2σ ±3σ standard deviation (σ) 1.0 mean (μ) 50 coverage intervals μ ± 1σ contains: 68.27% μ ± 2σ contains: 95.45% μ ± 3σ contains: 99.73% 05 sample vs population bessel's correction when estimating population sd from a sample, dividing by (n-1) instead of n produces an unbiased estimator . this correction accounts for the fact that sample variance systematically underestimates population variance. population sd σ = √(σ(xᵢ - μ)² / n) sample sd (corrected) s = √(σ(xᵢ - x̄)² / (n-1)) apply bessel's correction convergence demo observe how sample sd approaches population sd as sample size increases. the correction matters most for small samples. n = 10 resample 06 scope & limits scope of applicability ● interval or ratio scale data (meaningful distances) ● unimodal, approximately symmetric distributions ● contexts where outliers represent measurement error ● comparing variability across datasets with similar units structural limitations ● not applicable to nominal or ordinal data ● misleading for multimodal distributions ● cannot distinguish between different shapes with same spread ● exponentially sensitive to outliers (non-robust) failure mode simulator select a distribution type to see where standard deviation fails to capture the true structure of the data. bimodal skewed contaminated uniform the problem in a bimodal distribution, the mean falls between the two modes — a region with few or no observations. the standard deviation then measures spread around this meaningless central point, capturing neither the spread within each cluster nor the distance between clusters. better alternatives • report modes and their locations • use iqr or mad for robust spread • apply mixture model decomposition current distribution σ = 2.12 | mad = 1.48 07 diagnostic questions what happens if assumptions are violated? standard deviation remains mathematically computable for any set of real numbers. however, its epistemic meaning degrades: • skewed data: sd is pulled toward the tail, overstating "typical" spread • multimodal data: the mean is not representative, making sd meaningless • heavy tails: sd understates extreme event probability • outliers: single values can arbitrarily inflate sd what invariant does this tool rely on most critically? the assumption that the arithmetic mean is a meaningful center . this requires: • unimodal or symmetric distribution • data measured on interval/ratio scale • no extreme asymmetry in the underlying process without this, sd measures spread around a point that doesn't represent the data's central tendency. can different distributions produce the same sd? yes — infinitely many. this is a core limitation: sd is a lossy compression. examples with identical mean and sd: • normal distribution vs uniform distribution • bimodal vs unimodal distributions • symmetric vs moderately skewed distributions this is why sd should always be accompanied by visualization or additional measures. why square the deviations instead of using absolute values? squaring has both practical and theoretical justifications: • mathematical convenience: squared functions are differentiable everywhere • optimal estimation: mean minimizes sum of squared errors • theoretical foundations: central limit theorem involves variance • penalization: larger deviations are disproportionately weighted the alternative — mean absolute deviation (mad) — is more robust but has less convenient mathematical properties. 08 comparative
